name: Pure Land (Jingtu / Jōdo): birth in Amitābha's land
alt_names: Jōdokyō 浄土教 (Pure Land teaching, Japan)
regions: China (Lushan, Bingzhou/Xuanzhong si, Chang'an, Wutai, Hangzhou)

tradition.text: Amitābha attained buddhahood ten kalpas ago (Smaller & Larger Sūtras); in China the Lotus school counts from Huiyuan's vow on Lushan in 402 CE

scholarly.text: Sukhāvatī sūtras c. 1st–2nd c. CE; Chinese Pure Land as a self-conscious tradition from Tanluan, Daochuo and Shandao (6th–7th c.); lineage of 'patriarchs' constructed in the Song (Zongxiao 1200, Zhipan 1269)

transmissions_received.what: the Sukhāvatī sūtras, the Pratyutpanna-samādhi, the Contemplation Sūtra, the practice of recollecting buddhas (buddhānusmṛti)
Nāgārjuna's distinction of the difficult and easy paths; Tanluan's training in the Four Treatises (Sanlun) shapes 'the birth that is no birth'
Vasubandhu's Rebirth Treatise with its śamatha–vipaśyanā gates; the Mahāyānasaṃgraha's 'intention for another time' (occasion of debate)
the constantly-walking samādhi; Tiantai Pure Land commentaries and societies (Zunshi, Zhili, Chuandeng, Ouyi)
transmissions_received.evidence: Jingtu shiyi lun (attrib. Zhiyi); T1968, T1975

transmissions_given.what: Shandao's exclusive calling of the name, received by Hōnen in 1175
the seven masters' teaching of the primal vow and other-power, through Hōnen to Shinran
constantly-walking nenbutsu samādhi (brought by Ennin), Genshin's Ōjōyōshū
recitation of the name within Chan practice; dual cultivation; the 'who is reciting' huatou
the Ming Chan–Pure Land synthesis carried to Japan (1654)

distinctive_positions: Amitābha (Immeasurable Light, Immeasurable Life), who as the monk Dharmākara made vows, presides now over Sukhāvatī in the west; beings born there never fall back and attain awakening.
Birth (wangsheng / ōjō) in the Pure Land is the condition for completing the path: awakening is finished there, not here.
Practice centres on recollecting (nian) Amitābha — contemplating his body and land, and above all calling his name (chengming) — with faith and the aspiration to be born.
Nāgārjuna's easy path versus difficult path; Daochuo's two gates (the holy path and the Pure Land) matched to the last age of the Dharma.
Other-power (tali/tariki): birth is accomplished by the power of Amitābha's vow, not by one's own power (Tanluan), with differing degrees of emphasis in the later schools.

Even an evil-doer who calls the name ten times at death is born in the lowest grade (Contemplation Sūtra); the eighteenth vow excludes the five grave offenders and slanderers of the Dharma — reconciled by Shandao as restraint rather than rejection.
Later Chinese Pure Land joins recitation with Chan (dual cultivation) and reads the Pure Land also as mind-only while insisting on real birth in the West (Yanshou, Zhuhong, Ouyi).
summary: The Pure Land tradition teaches reliance on the buddha Amitābha and aspiration to be born in his land Sukhāvatī, where awakening is assured. Grounded in the Larger and Smaller Sukhāvatīvyūha and the Contemplation Sūtra, in Nāgārjuna's 'easy practice' and Vasubandhu's Rebirth Treatise, it became a self-conscious tradition in China through Tanluan (other-power), Daochuo (the last age; the two gates) and Shandao (the calling of the name as the rightly determined act), was later counted as a lineage of patriarchs beginning with Huiyuan of Lushan, merged with Chan and Tiantai practice in the Song–Ming, and in Japan passed through Genshin and the hijiri to the independent schools of Hōnen (Jōdo-shū), Shinran (Jōdo Shinshū), Ippen (Ji-shū) and Ryōnin (Yūzū Nenbutsu).

name: Jōdo-shū (the Pure Land school of Hōnen)
alt_names: the school of exclusive nenbutsu (senju nenbutsu)
regions: Japan (Kyoto: Chion-in, Kurodani Konkai Kōmyō-ji; Edo: Zōjō-ji; Kyushu)

tradition.text: founded in 1175 (Angen 1) when Hōnen, reading Shandao, turned to the exclusive nenbutsu

scholarly.text: late 12th c.; institutionalised under the Chinzei line from the 14th c.

transmissions_received.what: Hōnen's training on Mt Hiei; Genshin's Ōjōyōshū; the bodhisattva precepts transmitted in Jōdo-shū

transmissions_given.what: Hōnen's exclusive nenbutsu received by Shinran (1201)
Ippen trained in the Seizan line (Shōtatsu)

distinctive_positions: Of the two gates, set aside the holy path and enter the Pure Land gate; of the right and miscellaneous practices, set aside the miscellaneous and take the right; of the right, the calling of the name is the rightly determined act, because it accords with the Buddha's primal vow (Senchakushū).
The eighteenth vow 'selected' (senchaku) the nenbutsu as the one practice for birth, above all other practices, being both superior (the name holds all virtues) and easy (open to all).

The settled mind (anjin: the three minds of the Contemplation Sūtra), the practice undertaken (kigyō: the five right practices) and the manner of practice (sagyō: the four modes) — terms from Shandao.
Believe that birth is attained by even one calling, yet keep calling all one's life (Hōnen's letters).
At death Amitābha comes to welcome the practitioner (raigō); right mindfulness at death is sought.
Monastic and lay alike; the bodhisattva precepts (Tendai line) kept alongside the nenbutsu; the fivefold transmission (gojū sōden) as the school's rite of entrusting the teaching.
summary: The Jōdo school founded by Hōnen (1133–1212), who after decades of Tendai study found in Shandao's commentary that calling Amitābha's name wholeheartedly at all times is 'the rightly determined act, because it accords with the Buddha's vow', and taught exclusive nenbutsu to all, monastic and lay, good and evil. Its classic is the Senchakushū; its creed the One-Sheet Document. After persecution (1207, 1227) Hōnen's disciples formed lines — Chinzei (Benchō), Seizan (Shōkū), and the extinct lines of Kōsai, Ryūkan and Chōsai — of which Chinzei became the main body of modern Jōdo-shū.

name: Jōdo Shinshū (the True Pure Land school of Shinran)
regions: Japan (Kyoto: Nishi and Higashi Honganji; Kantō; Hokuriku; Mikawa)

tradition.text: founded in 1224 (Gennin 1), the year taken by Honganji as that of the Kyōgyōshinshō

scholarly.text: 13th c. (Shinran's communities in the Kantō); a school from Kakunyo's Honganji (14th c.), mass movement under Rennyo (15th c.)

transmissions_received.what: Hōnen's exclusive nenbutsu; permission to copy the Senchakushū (1205)
the seven masters: Nāgārjuna, Vasubandhu, Tanluan, Daochuo, Shandao, Genshin, Hōnen

distinctive_positions: Shinjin — the entrusting mind — is the true cause of birth; it is not produced by the practitioner but given (transferred) by Amida; the nenbutsu that follows is the expression of gratitude.
Both going to the Pure Land (ōsō) and returning to this world to save others (gensō) are Amida's transfer of merit.

At the moment shinjin is settled, one enters the rightly established state (shōjōju) in this life; birth in the true Pure Land at death is at once attaining great nirvāṇa; no deathbed welcome need be awaited.
The evil person is the true object of the vow: 'even a good person attains birth, how much more an evil person' (Tannishō 3).
Other practices and self-power nenbutsu lead only to the transformed land (19th and 20th vows); Shinran turned through the three vows to the eighteenth.
Jinen hōni: things become so of themselves by the working of the vow, free of the practitioner's calculation (hakarai).
Neither monk nor layman (hisō hizoku): married clergy, no precepts as condition of birth, no worship of other deities for worldly benefit, the name (myōgō) as object of reverence.
summary: The school descended from Shinran (1173–1263), Hōnen's disciple, who after exile (1207) lived as 'neither monk nor layman' among ordinary people in Echigo and the Kantō and in the Kyōgyōshinshō taught that teaching, practice, entrusting (shinjin) and realization are all Amida's transfer of merit to beings. Organised around Shinran's mausoleum (Honganji) by Kakunyo and spread by Rennyo's letters in the 15th c., it is today divided mainly into the Honganji (Nishi), Ōtani (Higashi) and Takada branches among the 'ten schools of Shinshū'.

name: Ji-shū (the Time school of Ippen)
regions: Japan (itinerant; head temple Shōjōkō-ji / Yugyō-ji, Fujisawa)

tradition.text: founded 1274 at Kumano, when Ippen received the oracle of the Kumano deity

scholarly.text: late 13th c.; organised as an order by Shinkyō after 1289

transmissions_received.what: Ippen's training under Shōtatsu, a disciple of Shōkū
Kūya's itinerant nenbutsu and 'casting off' as model

distinctive_positions: The birth of all beings was settled when Amida attained awakening ten kalpas ago; the name 'Namu Amida Butsu' itself is birth; the practitioner neither causes nor secures it.
Talismans (fusan) printed with the name are given to all, without choosing between those with and without faith, the pure and the impure (the Kumano oracle).
Casting off (sutete koso) everything — home, learning, even the thought of self and of faith — in the nenbutsu; a life of wandering (yugyō).
Dancing nenbutsu (odori nenbutsu) as joyful practice; recitation at the six times of day (whence 'Ji').
summary: The itinerant school of Ippen (1239–1289), who after the Kumano oracle of 1274 wandered through Japan distributing talismans inscribed 'Namu Amida Butsu — birth assured — six hundred thousand people' and leading dancing nenbutsu; he burned his writings at death. His successor Shinkyō organised the Ji-shū order, whose head bears the title Yugyō Shōnin.

name: Yūzū Nenbutsu-shū (the interfusing nenbutsu of Ryōnin)

tradition.text: 1117, when Amida revealed the interfusing nenbutsu to Ryōnin in samādhi

scholarly.text: early 12th c.; revived by Hōmyō in the 14th c. and recognised as a school in the Edo period

transmissions_received.what: Ryōnin's Tendai training and shōmyō chant (Ōhara)
interfusion of one and all (as understood by the school)

distinctive_positions: One person is all people, all people are one person; one practice is all practices, all practices are one practice: each person's nenbutsu interfuses with everyone's, so the merit of all is shared (the revelation verse, as transmitted).
Members inscribe their names in a register (myōchō) and pledge a daily number of recitations.
summary: The school of 'interfusing nenbutsu' traced to the Tendai chant master Ryōnin (1073–1132), to whom Amida is said to have revealed that one person's nenbutsu and all others' pervade one another; Ryōnin enrolled people of every class in a nenbutsu register. Revived in the 14th c. by Hōmyō; head temple Dainenbutsu-ji in Osaka.

name: Jōdo-shū Chinzei line
regions: Japan (Kyushu, then Kamakura and Kyoto; Chion-in, Zōjō-ji)
distinctive_positions: Nenbutsu is the practice of the primal vow; other practices can also lead to birth (shogyō ōjō) but are not the vow's own practice (as usually stated for Benchō's line).
Many-calling: continue the nenbutsu throughout life.
summary: The line of Hōnen's disciple Benchō (Shōkō-bō, 1162–1238), active in Kyushu (Chinzei), continued by Ryōchū (Nen'a); it became the mainstream of Jōdo-shū, with Chion-in and Zōjō-ji, and systematised the fivefold transmission (gojū sōden) under Shōgei.
notes: Chinzei doctrinal positions stated in general terms only; exact formulations to be checked.

name: Jōdo-shū Seizan line
regions: Japan (Nishiyama near Kyoto: Kōmyō-ji, Zenrin-ji/Eikandō, Seigan-ji)
distinctive_positions: All practices are taken up into (and have their meaning in) the nenbutsu; the Buddha's attainment ten kalpas ago and the beings' birth are one (as usually summarised for Shōkū's line).
summary: The line of Hōnen's disciple Shōkū (Zenne-bō, 1177–1247), who had Tendai esoteric training and taught at Nishiyama (Seizan) near Kyoto; Ippen's teacher Shōtatsu belonged to it. Today three Seizan schools (Jōdo-shū Seizan, Seizan Zenrinji-ha, Seizan Fukakusa-ha).
notes: Seizan doctrinal summary given only in general terms (low confidence on exact formulations).

name: Jōdo Shinshū Honganji-ha
distinctive_positions: Shares the Shinshū teaching of shinjin as the true cause of birth; differs institutionally, liturgically and in doctrinal-academy lineages rather than in core doctrine.
summary: The western branch of the Honganji after the split of 1602, when Kyōnyo was given land for a separate Honganji; head temple Nishi Honganji. The largest Shinshū body; led historically by Shinran's descendants.

name: Shinshū Ōtani-ha
distinctive_positions: Shares the Shinshū teaching of shinjin as the true cause of birth; differs institutionally, liturgically and in doctrinal-academy lineages rather than in core doctrine.
summary: The eastern branch of the Honganji, from Kyōnyo (1558–1614), who received land from Tokugawa Ieyasu in 1602; head temple Higashi Honganji; home of the Meiji reform movement of Kiyozawa Manshi.

name: Shinshū Takada-ha
distinctive_positions: Shares the Shinshū teaching of shinjin as the true cause of birth; differs institutionally, liturgically and in doctrinal-academy lineages rather than in core doctrine.
summary: Branch descending from Shinran's Kantō disciple Shinbutsu of Takada (Shimotsuke); head temple Senju-ji, moved to Isshinden (Ise) in the 15th c.; preserves early manuscripts of Shinran.

name: The White Lotus school of Mao Ziyuan (Bailian zong)

scholarly.text: 12th c. (Mao Ziyuan d. 1166) to Yuan; later 'White Lotus' sects of the Ming–Qing are distinct and partly millenarian

distinctive_positions: Lay societies keeping the five precepts, confirmed by five recitations of Amitābha's name; repentance halls; Tiantai-style 'four lands and three contemplations'.
summary: Lay Pure Land repentance societies founded by the monk Mao Ziyuan (Cizhao zongzhu, d. 1166) on the model of Huiyuan's Lotus society; repeatedly banned, defended by Pudu's Lushan lianzong baojian (1305). The later 'White Lotus teachings' of Ming–Qing sectarian religion took the name but are outside this entry.
notes: Scope limited to the Song–Yuan Buddhist societies as described in T1973.
